newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian gov't submits bill to strip court power.
newsitem.headline: Colombian gov't submits bill to strip court power.

text.p: A Columbian government minister submitted a bill to Congress on Tuesday that aims to strip the nation's Constitutional Court of the power to determine when a president is able to rule by decree.

The bill, presented by Interior Minister Horacio Serpa and which some political analysts fear would give President Ernesto Samper virtual dictatorial powers, was drawn up after last week's vote by the court overturning the government's three-month-old state of economic emergency on grounds it was unconstitutional.

Government finances were left in disarray by the court ruling. Samper, who has been dogged by allegations that he used drug money to finance his presidential campaign, said he had no doubt that it was politically motivated.
"This bill is not a revenge measure, nor do I think it is dictatorial. We're just trying to put thngs in their proper persepctive," Serpa told reporters after presenting the bill.

If the legislation is approved by Congress, which is dominated by Samper's Liberal Party, the court would be permitted to rule on whether emergency decress were constitutional but would no longer have the authority to decide under which situations a state of emergency could be declared.
This would in effect open the way for the president to make a wider use of emergency rule and ram through measures -- including economic austerity plans -- without the prior approval of Congress.

Under the current system of checks and balances, the Constitutional Court is the final arbiter of when the executive branch is legitimately empowered to declare a state of emergency and rule by decree.
In its ruling last week, the Constitutional Court decided the emergency declared in mid-January was not caused by unforeseen circumstances but was a gradual accumulation of macroeconomic factors.

"This bill will allow the court to consider the constitutionality of decrees issued but it will mean the court doesn't have the responsibility to examine the constitutionality of the declaration of the state of emergency," Serpa said.
